items.followUp: Why is AlCl₃ considered electron deficient?

rubric.why: The key reason is that boron has only six electrons around it in BF₃.
rubric.description: States that boron has only six electrons in its valence shell in BF₃.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the six-electron valence shell.

rubric.why: An incomplete octet explains the electron deficiency and boron’s ability to accept a lone pair.
rubric.description: Explains that boron has an incomplete octet and can accept a lone pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the incomplete octet or its consequence.

modelAnswer: In BF₃, boron forms three covalent bonds and has only six electrons in its valence shell.
Its octet is incomplete, so BF₃ is electron deficient and can accept a lone pair of electrons.

items.followUp: Define amorphous solids and give two examples.

rubric.why: A regular, orderly arrangement of particles is the defining feature of crystalline solids.
rubric.description: Defines crystalline solids by the regular arrangement of their particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear definition involving an orderly arrangement.

rubric.why: The question asks for examples as well as the definition.
rubric.description: Gives two valid examples of crystalline solids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correct examples.

modelAnswer: Crystalline solids are solids whose particles are arranged in a regular, orderly pattern.
Examples include sodium chloride and quartz.

rubric.why: Condensation is the change from the gaseous state to the liquid state.
rubric.description: States that a gas or vapour changes into a liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the change of state.

rubric.why: Cooling or heat loss commonly brings about condensation.
rubric.description: Mentions cooling or removal of heat as the condition for condensation.

modelAnswer: Condensation is the change of a gas or vapour into a liquid.
It occurs when the gas is cooled or loses heat.

rubric.why: The m/v unit expresses the mass of solute relative to the volume of solution.
rubric.description: Identifies m/v percentage as a mass of solute per volume of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating solute mass to solution volume.

rubric.why: A correct numerical example makes the meaning of the percentage clear.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as 5 g of solute in 100 mL of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example with the stated units.

modelAnswer: The m/v % concentration is the number of grams of solute present in 100 mL of solution.
For example, a 5% m/v glucose solution contains 5 g of glucose in 100 mL of solution.

items.followUp: Give two examples of a gas in liquid solution.

rubric.why: Fog and mist are examples of liquid droplets dispersed in a gas.
rubric.description: Gives one valid liquid-in-gas example: fog or mist.
Gives both fog and mist as examples.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both examples.

modelAnswer: Fog is a liquid-in-gas solution: tiny water droplets are dispersed in air.
Mist is another example of a liquid-in-gas solution.

items.followUp: What is an alloy? Give one example.

rubric.why: Alloying involves combining a metal with another element to make an alloy.
rubric.description: Defines alloying as mixing a metal with one or more other elements, usually in the molten state.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the mixing process or the resulting mixture.

rubric.why: A valid example demonstrates the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a correct alloy example, such as brass (copper and zinc).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: Alloying is the process of mixing a metal with one or more other elements, usually in the molten state, to form an alloy.
Brass, made from copper and zinc, is an example.

items.followUp: Define oxidation number and state the oxidation number of oxygen in H₂O.

rubric.why: Oxidation number represents the apparent charge assigned to an atom in a compound or ion.
rubric.description: Defines oxidation number as the apparent or assigned charge of an atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear definition.

rubric.why: The example must correctly apply the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as Na having oxidation number +1 in NaCl.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct atom, compound and oxidation number.

modelAnswer: Oxidation number is the apparent charge assigned to an atom in a molecule or ion.
For example, the oxidation number of sodium in NaCl is +1.

items.followUp: Why are copper and iron more reactive than gold?

accept: low tendency to form positive ions
rubric.why: Metals are reactive when they readily lose electrons; silver and gold do so with difficulty.
rubric.description: States that silver and gold have a low tendency to lose electrons or form positive ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining their low tendency to undergo oxidation.

rubric.why: Their position in the reactivity series or occurrence in the native state reflects their low reactivity.
rubric.description: Connects their low reactivity with their position in the reactivity series or their occurrence uncombined in nature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid supporting explanation.

modelAnswer: Silver and gold have a very low tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.
They are near the bottom of the reactivity series and may occur in the native state.
